newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostages well despite blast, long captivity.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostages well despite blast, long captivity.

text.p: The 103 hostages held by Marxist rebels inside the Japanese ambassador's home in Peru are in good health despite nine days of captivity, a Catholic bishop who visited them on Thursday said.

A loud explosion in the middle of the night on Thursday had led to fears for the safety of the mainly VIP hostages. But Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani told reporters after entering the building that the captives were not hurt.
"They are well, they are calm, they are firm," he said.
Red Cross officials said the mystery blast may have been caused by an animal stepping on a mine near the building.

Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holding the residence are armed with grenades, explosives and ample ammunition and have booby-trapped entrances to the grand two-storey building, released hostages have said.
Cipriani, the bishop of Ayacucho, first visited the residence (on) Christmas Day to celebrate mass with the captives, hear confessions and share a turkey lunch donated by Peru's first family.
Emerging for a second time on Thursday, he appealed to the rebels to examine their consciences and end the siege.
"Let us hope that their hearts will be moved," Cipriani said. Pope John Paul was following the crisis closely and praying for the victims, he added.
Although churchmen say Cipriani is a conservative who is close to President Alberto Fujimori, the bishop denied he had been involved in any negotiations beyond his pastoral mission to the captives.

The rebels have released roughly 400 of the hostages they initially took but have kept those they consider most useful as bargaining chips, including top Peruvian government officials, ambassadors and Japanese businessmen.

Half an hour before he spoke, the rebels freed Guatemalan ambassador Jose Maria Argueta, the first liberation of a hostage since a Japanese diplomat was released for health reasons on Wednesday evening.

Looking well, Argueta told reporters that the guerrillas wanted to show their support for the forthcoming peace treaty between Guatemala's government and the country's URNG rebels, to be signed on Dec. 29.

After Argueta left, Red Cross workers cleared away sacks of rubbish from the residence and brought in fresh supplies of food and water but there was still no sign of a major breakthrough to end the crisis.

Isaac Velazco, the MRTA's self-styled international spokesman, told Reuters by telephone from Hamburg, Germany that his comrades in the residence would hold out for as long as it took to secure their main demand -- the release of rebels held in Peruvian jails.
"We will be waiting. The Peruvian people have suffered 500 years of exploitation so we have all the time in the world," he said.

The MRTA takes its name from Tupac Amaru, an Indian leader who led a bloody but unsuccessful rebellion against Spanish colonial rule in 1780-81 and was executed by being drawn and quartered in a public square.

Fujimori has flatly rejected the rebels' demands, telling them to lay down their arms and release their captives if they want to avoid the use of force. Velazco accused the government of "provoking a bloody, military solution" instead of negotiating.
The crisis began when the rebels stormed the residence during a smart cocktail party on Dec. 19 honouring the Japanese emperor's birthday. Around 30 of the remaining hostages are Japanese.

In a sign Tokyo expects the crisis to drag on, Foreign Ministry officials said Japan's prime minister and foreign minister were both considering cancelling foreign trips planned for January because of the continuing hostage crisis.

Fujimori has turned down foreign offers of military help and Russian president Boris Yeltsin's suggestion on Wednesday of sending a special G-7 task force to free the hostages brought no immediate official response from Lima.
